chief_complaint: progressive shortness of breath, ankle swelling, and fatigue for 1 month
hpi_details: A 29-year-old male presents to the clinic with progressive shortness of breath, ankle swelling, and fatigue for 1 month, gradually worsening. He has no known prior heart disease, and denies any preceding viral illness, recreational drug use, or family history of heart problems that he is aware of.
ideas: He thinks his kidneys are failing because his body is suddenly holding onto so much fluid.
concerns: He is worried he will lose his job at the warehouse if he cannot stay on his feet and lift heavy boxes.
expectations: He hopes to be prescribed water pills to reduce the swelling in his ankles and get blood tests to check his organs.

investigation_events.title: NT-proBNP and echocardiogram
investigation_events.availability_message: The heart failure blood test and echocardiogram are now available.

results.value: Dilated left ventricle with global hypokinesia; LVEF 30%; no significant valvular disease

clinical_knowledge.topic: Congestive Heart Failure evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Congestive Heart Failure is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes obtaining BNP, chest X-ray, and echocardiography, and, because this is a young patient without typical risk factors, actively searching for a non-ischaemic cause (myocarditis, familial/genetic cardiomyopathy, thyroid disease, or substance use) rather than assuming ischaemic heart failure, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: progressive shortness of breath, ankle swelling, and fatigue for 1 month

Key HPI features: A 29-year-old male presents to the clinic with progressive shortness of breath, ankle swelling, and fatigue for 1 month, gradually worsening. He has no known prior heart disease, and denies any preceding viral illness, recreational drug use, or family history of heart problems that he is aware of.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals and volume status (JVP, lung crackles, peripheral oedema). Cardiac auscultation for S3 gallop or murmurs. BNP/NT-proBNP, chest X-ray, and echocardiogram to confirm heart failure and assess ejection fraction; in a young adult, also screen for treatable causes with TSH, viral serology history, and a family/substance-use history.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Congestive Heart Failure.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Breathlessness at rest, or waking at night gasping.
management_principles: Obtain BNP, chest X-ray, and echocardiogram; in a young adult without typical risk factors, screen for non-ischaemic causes (myocarditis, familial cardiomyopathy, thyroid disease, substance use)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of progressive shortness of breath, ankle swelling, and fatigue for 1 month. HPI: systolic/diastolic dysfunction.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals and volume status (JVP, lung crackles, peripheral oedema). Cardiac auscultation for S3 gallop or murmurs. BNP/NT-proBNP, chest X-ray, and echocardiogram to confirm heart failure and assess ejection fraction; in a young adult, also screen for treatable causes with TSH, viral serology history, and a family/substance-use history.
reference_soap.assessment: New-onset Congestive Heart Failure in a 29-year-old man; given his age and absence of traditional cardiovascular risk factors, a non-ischaemic cause (myocarditis, familial/genetic dilated cardiomyopathy, thyroid disease, or substance-induced cardiomyopathy) must be actively sought rather than assumed to be ischaemic.
reference_soap.plan: Obtain BNP, chest X-ray, and echocardiogram; screen for non-ischaemic causes (myocarditis, familial cardiomyopathy, thyroid disease, substance use). Start oral Furosemide, titrate GDMT. Consult specialist if symptoms worsen. Counsel patient.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Congestive Heart Failure
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Congestive Heart Failure
Implement evidence-based management plan: Obtain BNP, chest X-ray, Echo. Start oral Furosemide, titrate GDMT

teaching.one_liner: The heart cannot pump enough for the body's needs, so fluid backs up — breathlessness, ankle swelling and fatigue together.
red_flags: Breathlessness at rest, or waking at night gasping

must_ask.say: How far can you walk on the flat before you need to stop?
Do you get breathless lying flat? How many pillows do you use?
Have your ankles or legs been swelling?
Do you wake in the night short of breath and have to sit up?
Has your weight gone up quickly in the last week or two?
What medications are you taking at the moment?

must_ask.objective: Possible cause in a young patient
must_ask.say: Have you had a recent viral illness, do you use any recreational drugs, or does anyone in your family have heart problems or an unexplained sudden death?

history.answer: I've been feeling increasingly short of breath and noticed my ankles have been swelling up over the past month, and I feel completely exhausted.
It started gradually about a month ago and has been steadily getting worse each week.
At first I only noticed it when jogging, but now climbing just one flight of stairs or walking a short block leaves me breathless.
It is mostly constant during the day whenever I exert myself, and I have never experienced anything like this before.
Yes, over the past couple of weeks I cannot sleep flat and have to prop myself up with two or three pillows to breathe comfortably.
Yes, a few times this past week I woke up in the middle of the night gasping for air and had to sit upright by the open window.
Walking, climbing stairs, or any physical effort makes it worse, while sitting completely still helps me catch my breath a bit.
No, I haven't heard any wheezing or whistling sounds when I breathe.
I have had a mild, dry cough especially when lying down, but no phlegm and definitely no fever or chills.
No, I haven't had any tight squeezing chest pressure or sharp stabbing pain when I breathe.
My heart sometimes feels like it's racing slightly when I walk, but I haven't had fainting spells or severe dizziness.
No, I have never coughed up blood.
Both of my ankles have become puffy and swollen over the past few weeks, and socks leave deep dents in my skin.
I weighed myself a few days ago and realized I've gained about four kilograms over the past month, even though I'm eating less.
No, both legs look equal and I have not had calf pain, recent surgeries, long flights, or bed rest.
I feel drained of energy all day long, but I haven't seen any pale skin, black tarry stools, or unusual bleeding.
No, I don't get numbness or tingling around my mouth or hands, and this breathlessness isn't caused by panic or stress.
No, I have never been diagnosed with high blood pressure, asthma, heart attacks, or any lung condition.
No, I have never used an inhaler or asthma spray.
I work in an office at a computer and haven't been exposed to dust, asbestos, birds, or mold.
No, I don't take beta blockers, aspirin, pain relievers, chemotherapy, or any other regular pills.
No, I haven't had a flu, heavy cold, sore throat, or diarrhea in the months leading up to this.
No, I haven't noticed heat intolerance, excessive sweating, hand tremors, or changes in my neck.
I was wondering if my kidneys are shutting down, since my legs and ankles are swelling up like balloons.
I'm really worried I'll lose my warehouse job if I can't stay on my feet all day.
I'm hoping you can give me some water pills to get rid of this swelling and run some blood tests.
I've always been healthy and have no history of chronic medical conditions.
I have never had surgery and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I am not taking any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or herbal supplements.
I have no known allergies to medications, foods, or anything else.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used vape products.
I only have a beer or two occasionally when out with friends, maybe once or twice a month.
No, I have never used cocaine, methamphetamine, or any recreational or illicit drugs.
I work as a software administrator and live in an apartment with my partner.
No one in my family has had heart failure or died suddenly at a young age that I am aware of.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, heart rate 92 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, temperature 36.7°C.
Mild respiratory effort at rest; no central or peripheral cyanosis, and no digital clubbing.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor; sclerae are non-icteric.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, smooth, and non-tender without palpable nodules or bruits.
Elevated jugular venous distension noted approximately 4 cm above the sternal angle at 45 degrees.
Symmetrical chest expansion; apex beat is laterally displaced to the 6th intercostal space outside the midclavicular line.
Bilateral basal resonance slightly decreased; mild dullness to percussion at both lung bases.
Fine inspiratory crackles auscultated at bilateral lung bases; no wheezes or stridor heard.
Regular rhythm with an audible S3 gallop; normal S1 and S2, without murmurs or pericardial friction rubs.
Abdomen is soft with mild tenderness over the liver edge 2 cm below the right costal margin; hepatojugular reflux is positive.
Bilateral symmetric 2+ pitting edema present over both ankles and shins.
Calves are symmetrical without unilateral swelling, warmth, cord sign, or calf tenderness.
